comment_text: Very interesting — especially the impact of autocorrelation. In practice, this is exactly what makes PD validation tricky. We often assume independence when applying statistical tests, but default rates are clearly driven by common macro factors. This creates a real risk of misinterpreting validation results — especially with short time series. Curious if you’ve explored alternatives that are more robust to correlation?

author: Andrija Djurovic
author_headline: Risk Advisory
comment_text: Sauran Sarbassov thanks for your comment. Yes, I have investigated some adjustments to account for correlation of defaults across reference dates. I plan to post about this together with the new multi-period average testing approach. It is indeed a very interesting topic. Practitioners often consider correlation over time mainly when running regressions in the context of PD modeling, but it is equally important in other areas, such as testing and MoC within the IRB framework. In essence, correlation affects the effective sample size and is therefore directly related to statistical testing as well.

author: Nikola Perović, FRM
author_headline: Quantitative Analyst.
comment_text: Sauran Sarbassov Also see Order statistic test [Blümke] which incorporates the time-series of 1Y default rates at rating grade or portfolio level, into the evaluation. If the rank order of the most recent 1Y default rate is "low", more summation terms are added to the calculation. If the rank is "high", less summation terms are considered. The analogy is with that of driving a vehicle with automatic transmission - where depending on the terrain and target provided [to the tempomat], the engine has to overcompensate when driving uphill [to reach and maintain a certain speed level] and undercompensate on the downhill. Of course, other variations can be explored, with recursive logic for the RDS etc. Unfortunately, the original test still uses the usual 1-factor copula conditional PDs. One can replace those with custom conditional distributions based on empirical CDFs, for the calculation. Cheers.

author: Sauran Sarbassov

comment_text: Nikola Perović, FRM Thanks for sharing — very insightful. The idea of incorporating time dynamics is particularly interesting, especially given how sensitive these tests are to correlation and small sample effects. Using multiple periods seems helpful in stabilising the signal, though the dependence structure itself likely remains. I also find it quite interesting that tests like Blümke effectively rely on ranking (i.e. discrimination) to assess calibration — a subtle but powerful idea. Makes you wonder to what extent test rejections reflect true miscalibration versus dependence effects. Will definitely take a closer look.

author: Bul Ekici
author_headline: Independent Macro & Markets Strategist | Former Central Bank Economist | FX & Fixed Income Analyst
comment_text: Thank you Jakob, you raise a valid point. There are, however, several studies (including Engel & Wu’s own paper and more recent work by Chen & Chou 2023) that show models augmented with liquidity yields are not purely retrospective: they can deliver some out-of-sample predictive power, particularly over multi-quarter horizons. That said, the caveats matter. The predictability is not stable across currencies or time periods, and the framework is far better suited for risk-exposure quantification over 1–5 years than for short-term directional forecasting. In a risk-management setting, I find its real value is in the structural decomposition and scenario analysis it enables (interest-rate differentials plus liquidity/risk premia), rather than in trying to beat a random walk from month to month. Thanks again, great discussion.
